articles.text: P i e d m o n t C o m m u n i t y Church’s (PCC) annual Mexico House Building trip over Spring break, a popular rite of passage for hundreds of teens for many years, will not occur this year. Senior Pastor Steve Schibsted sent a letter to past participants in the summer of 2024 relaying the decision to put a pause on the trip. The leader of the Mexico Trip, Director of Student Ministries Scott Kail, is no longer with the Church. It appears he retired on June 7, 2024. Kail led the trip for 19 years. Its popularity grew to include more than 200 teens and adults to build 12 homes for locals in Tijuana’s Valle de Palmas. The Aqua Team shares the shade with local residents in Valle de Palmas, Mexico, by a newly constructed home. “With the absence of [Kail’s] leadership, I am writing to let you know that we are going to push pause on the trip this coming year,” Senior Pastor Schibsted wrote. “The trip is a huge undertaking for our church. We don’t see any way that we could orchestrate the trip this year without Scott.” The restructuring of the church, without Kail, and without finding a replacement, suggests that there are other reasons causing the church to rethink the trip. Schibsted said no one from the church offered to take over leadership of the trip. “We really just questioned if sending kids for over $2000 for a mission trip was really the right thing to do,” Schibsted told the Post. Despite the complexities and the high price tag participants loved the experience. “I am a junior and have gone since my freshman year. I was looking forward to going one more year before I got to be a leader. I really hope they bring it back next year,” said Dahlia Osman.
articles.title: Mexico house-building trip for teens canceled

articles.text: The Community Engagement Committee of the Piedmont Education Foundation (PEF) welcomes Piedmont neighbors to enjoy cocktails and conversation with former Ambassador to Australia Jeff Bleich at the Piedmont home of Ellen and Pete Wilson the evening of Wednesday, April 16, at 7:30 p.m. Jeff Bleich’s legal career includes serving in the White House as special counsel to President Obama, law clerk to the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court and president of the State Bar of California. Additionally he has served as chair of the California State University Board of Trustees, chair of the Fulbright Foreign Scholarship Board, and as a trustee of Amherst College. Bleich also served as the United States ambassador to Australia and as a senior advisor to the Director of National Intelligence. He is an ambassadorial fellow at the University of Sydney, chairs the board of the Bleich Centre of Democracy and Disruptive Technologies in Adelaide and is a professorial fellow at Flinders University also in Adelaide. Bleich earned a BA from Amherst College, MPP from Harvard University, JD from UC Berkeley and honorary doctorates from SFSU and two Australian universities. Currently Bleich is a Visiting Scholar at Stanford’s Center for Advanced Study in Behavioral Sciences where he is completing two books. Bleich’s writings have focused principally on democracy, international relations and constitutional law. A product of public schools, Jeff and his wife, Becky Bleich, are committed to public educaPiedmont resident Jeff Bleich tion and are delighted to help raise funds for Piedmont schools. When they were not living abroad, their three children all attended Piedmont schools. Bleich’s remarks on the evening of April 16 will focus on what is behind the fall in democracy worldwide, the rise in autocracy, and his current book project updating Machiavelli’s “The Prince” for modern times. Bleich’s recent article in Persuasion offers a glimpse of how Machiavelli’s advice to autocrats explains recent events. In a March 18 article, Bleich focused his attention on the judiciary branch and the limits of Presidential power under the constitution. Tax deductible tickets are available at the Piedmont Store for $75, at https://piedmontstore. org/products/cocktails-conversation-with-jeff-bleich. Thanks to many generous donations, 100% of the proceeds raised from the event will go to supporting Piedmont Schools. articles.text: Gorgeous, loving Alabama may be the tortie you’ve been waiting for. This female DSH who is almost two years old is very playful. She carefully stalks her favorite stuffed toy before catching it and parading it around the room with a series of short meows. She also loves running back and forth after her rainbow ribbon toy. She can be a little shy with new people, but once she feels safe, she’s an affectionate young companion. Alabama might do well with another cat but prefers to live in a home without dogs. She requires a wet food diet and medication to manage pain from an old injury, which she happily eats tucked into her dinner. This young miss also likes gentle petting, but asks that you avoid her sensitive spots, so she’s hoping for an adopter with a little cat experience. Show her love and she’ll return it – her fosters report Alabama, a two-year-old cat, is now available for adoption. she’ll flop to the ground and make air biscuits when you say her name! articles.text: The Honorable Mary-Margaret Anderson, a retired administrative law judge with the California Office of Administrative Hearings, is now serving as chair of The National Judicial College Board of Trustees. The College is the nation’s oldest, largest and most widely attended school for judges. Judge Anderson first joined the board in 2016 and was elected by her fellow board members to serve a one- year term as chair starting in January 2025. “The mission of the NJC is to both educate and inspire the judiciary,” Judge Anderson said. “Now more than ever, we must support our nation’s judges. By doing so, we support an institution that is essential to our democracy. Without fair, impartial, competent and independent judges, democracy is impossible. I am enormously proud of the work the NJC does and to serve as its board chair.” At the Office of Administrative Hearings Judge Anderson presided over the full range of cases brought by state, county, and local agencies, including school districts, from 1997 until her retirement in 2017. Judge Anderson is a past president of the National Association of Administrative Law Judiciary (NAALJ). She also served on the Judges’ Journal Editorial Board, the quarterly magazine published by the American Bar Association’s Judicial Division, for eight years, the last two as co-chair. She is currently co-chair of the Judge Mary-Margaret Anderson Judicial Division’s Book Editorial Board. She has taught ethics, evidence, and expert evidence to new and experienced judges in a variety of settings. Judge Anderson has resided in Piedmont since 1976 with her husband Lannie Spencer. Their sons Brett and Scott attended the Piedmont schools. About the National Judicial College The National Judicial College was founded in 1963 and is based at the University of Nevada, Reno. It trains judges nationwide, improving the delivery of justice and advancing the rule of law through a process of professional study and collegial dialogue. The College offers an average of 100 courses and programs annually with more than 12,000 judges attending from all 50 states and more than 150 countries. open every day 8:30 am – 3 pm

articles.text: You’re right: to be happy. To be healthy is #2. Right again? Yup, “happy” here doesn’t mean ephemeral pleasures, such as a tasty meal, a good cup of coffee, a ‘frivolous’ book, a movie, getting a nice car, gambling, or watching sports. Last pop quiz: If you could only ask one question to figure out if someone will be happy today, what would it be? Okay, a few possibilities popped into your mind this time, right? Let’s come back to that and offer the answer. In a Gallup World survey of 1,551,362 adults collected from 164 nations – the largest, most representative sample of the world’s population, the best predictor of the amount of positive emotions felt today was: “Did you learn something new yesterday?” Interesting, right? But, so what? Learning something is meaningful, and meaning is what creates a life of joy, which is truly what parents wish for their children, above all. In exploring how individuals find meaning in life—essentially, how they discover sustained fulfillment and joy—it is apparent that there are four cornerstones central to this pursuit: Discovery, Expression, Service, and Love. 1. Discovery: This involves a continual quest for personal understanding and the exploration of one’s desires and capacities. It’s about unraveling the layers of who we are and what we truly seek from life. 2. Expression: Stemming from the insights gained through self-discovery, expression is the process of showcasing our inner selves to the world. This can be through art, communication, or any form that allows one to convey their personal essence. 3. Service: This cornerstone asks, “How can I contribute to the betterment of others?” It is about extending oneself beyond personal needs to aid and uplift others, thereby enriching the communal human experience. Purpose is central to meaning, and after happiness and health, it is the 3rd most wished for by parents. 4. Love: Representing deep connections and affections, love may be directed towards people, places, or things. It is a profound force that drives much of human interaction and fulfillment. These cornerstones manifest differently depending on one’s life stage, cultural background, and personal circumstances. For instance, a monk might prioritize service and love, while a young adult may focus more intensely on discovery and expression. The cultural environment also plays a significant role in shaping which cornerstone predominates in an individual’s life. The people around us act as branches supporting our life’s tree, providing context and meaning. While not inherently meaningful—similar to being alone in a crowd or having numerous online contacts with few deep connections—the true value in relationships comes through these cornerstones. They help us discover ourselves, express our inner thoughts, commit acts of service, and experience love. The depth of these relationships, much like the thickness of branches, determines their impact on our lives, influencing how we find meaning and joy. However, finding and sustaining this sense of meaning is not without challenges. Fear is a significant hindrance; it stifles our ability to engage with life’s cornerstones by shifting our focus towards immediate safety and comfort. Another less obvious obstacle is the pursuit of fleeting happiness, which can distract from the deeper, more fulfilling joy that comes from engaging with our foundational cornerstones. these four cornerstones, individuals can transcend the ordinary, finding not just happiness but profound joy and fulfillment in their lives. For more resources on creating a meaningful life, visit the nonprofit organization ameaningoflife.org, a comprehensive platform dedicated to helping individuals live more purposefully and joyfully. Randall Grayson, Ph.D. (psychology) has been Camp Augusta’s director for over 20 years and is excited to share AMeaningOfLife.org with the world.

The business, located at 4400 Piedmont Ave., will host a grand reopening celebration within the next three weeks to mark its return to serving Piedmont-area drivers. Staff training began this week on April 1. All staff returning for training worked there prior to the closure in 2023. “That’s a testimony to the kind of people that come in there and get their car washed, because they wouldn’t come back to a place that didn’t have nice people as customers,” said owner Carla Betts. According to Betts, the car wash is fully operational, but additional improvements are planned, including the installation of two shade structures after the grand opening to provide sun protection for both staff and customers. The car wash will resume full-service cleaning options, offering both hand and machine washes. Business hours will remain the same: 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. Although an exact reopening date has not been announced, the celebration is expected to include balloons, music and an ice cream truck. Betts expressed appreciation for the community’s support during the closure. “I just thank them for the continual questions of ‘When are you going to open?’ They started asking those the day after we closed… and the questions have never stopped,” she said. “That just goes to show that we’ve been missed.” Workers prepare the Betts Car Wash for its opening later this month.

articles.text: Three Chevron gas stations were targeted in attempted “crash & grab” burglaries in the early morning of Tuesday, March 11. Located on Lakeshore Avenue, Redwood Road, and Moraga Avenue, the stations were all broken into within 45 minutes of each other around 3:30 a.m. The burglars, seemingly looking to steal the safe at each station, crashed cars into the stores of two of the stations and broke the window to access another. $250,000-$300,000 in estimated damages resulted from the break-ins, although the criminals escaped empty handed as police arrived. “All of the electrical stuff is gone, all of the computer driven stuff is gone, and they’ve gotten absolutely nothing,” said owner and Piedmont resident Carla Betts. “Within 45 minutes they hit three of our places and just did massive damage to the building and got absolutely nothing – they didn’t even steal a Red Bull.” It is possible the Lakeshore station’s store may not be opening again. “The store on Lakeshore is not open. And I don’t think we’re going to re-open it,” said Betts. According to Betts, the attempted burglaries fall in line with similar stories from other gas stations across Oakland and its neighboring cities. “They’re targeting any small business that they consider a soft target,” said manager Rick Draper in an interview with CBS News. “It’s just a sad thing that this is repeating itself all over the city virtually all the time.” The burglars’ escape raises questions about the effectiveness of Oakland Police Department’s no pursuit policy. “I don’t know where I stand [on the pursuit policy], because I don’t want them pursuing people and hitting a random child or a random pedestrian. That’s not fair. I care about those families. I also care about my business,” said Operations Manager Marissa Betts in an interview with NBC News. articles.text: Piedmont suffered a 14-4 loss to Berkeley. Piedmont’s boys’ lacrosse team suffered a rough 14-4 loss to Berkeley at Witter Field on Friday, March 28. It was their fifth straight loss. The result came against last year’s Western Alameda County Conference champions and the current No. 1 team in the league. The Highlanders are 2-1 in the league and can clinch a berth in the North Coast Section playoffs by finishing with an even overall or league record. Piedmont will host Bishop O’Dowd on Friday, April 4 in a critical league match. The Dragons are 6-4, but have faced weaker teams than Piedmont’s difficult schedule, which has been wrought with D1 schools like Amador Valley, Casa Grande, Campolindo, and Berkeley. 14-4 loss to Berkeley It was actually a strong first quarter for the Highlanders, trailing 3-2 at the end of the opening 12 minutes but was held scoreless through the second and third quarters. In the first quarter, Piedmont opened the game with a goal straight out of the faceoff. Connor Fredericks won one of his 14 draws, turning it up field to long stick midfielder P.J. Brayer for a goal just 18 seconds into the game. But from there, Berkeley scored three straight goals with 9:51, 9:31, and 2:57 left in the first quarter. Piedmont got one back when Ian Nguyen scored with 28 second seconds left, but it marked the Highlanders’ last time to score until the fourth quarter. What transpired was PHS Staff Photos Goalie Gus Von Metzsch moves the ball upfield. He had 16 saves. Connor Fredericks lines up a shot. He scored twice and won 14 face-offs. struggling to move the ball in transition and maintaining possession through an aggressive press while in the attacking zone—resulting in offense relying on goalie Gus Von Metszch to move the ball toward midfield. Turnovers are an issue that has plagued the Highlanders since transitioning from former coach Al Yu following the school’s D2 NCS Championship appearance in 2023. Piedmont had a couple looks in the second quarter before BHS started to continuously force turnovers. Timmy Kalamas had a shot blocked with 6:25 left, but it led to a Berkeley goal in transition. Fredericks then had a pair of shots go wide while Gianluca Richmond had a shot hit the post with 5:15 on the clock Berkeley scored a little over a minute later. After that, Piedmont committed four turnovers without taking a shot, leading to a Berkeley goal with 18 seconds left. Brayer and Fredericks had shots go wide with 9:43 and 9:17 left, but the attack commit a costly turnover with 8:42 left, leading to a Berkeley got on the ensuing possession. Kalamas had a shot on target with 7:10 left, while Brayer and Fredericks also had shots saved four minutes later. Berkeley scored twice in the last 25 seconds before halftime. In the fourth, Piedmont got back on the board with 8:30 left, but Berkeley scored straight out of the faceoff 16 seconds later. The Jackets scored another four goals until Fredericks netted another with 40 seconds left. Final stats: Fredericks scored twice with seven ground balls and won 14/17 face-offs. Brayer scored once and gathered six ground balls. Nguyen scored once and pickd up six ground balls. Kalamas had two assists. Von Metzsch was busy with 16 saves. articles.text: Piedmont High’s boys’ tennis team dropped a pair of matches and its match on Monday with Head-Royce was rained out. PHS lost 6-1 to Bishop O’Dowd at the Corey Reich Tennis Center on Tuesday, March 25, and to Lick-Wilmerding on Friday, March 28 also at home. Piedmont’s wins in the two matches came from Lucas Smolko at No. 1 singles against O’Dowd, and at No. 1 doubles duo of Gianluca Bini and Luca LaForte won against Lick. For Smolko, he won 7-5, 7-5 over Neo Chai, who Lucas defeated in last year’s Western Alameda County Conference Individual Tournament for the singles title. Tuesday’s meeting could be another preview of this year’s singles final once again. “Our sole win was Lucas at #1 singles, It was a nice win because Neo is a very strong player who always gives Lucas a run for his Monday,” coach Jim Landes said. Bini and LaForte won handily in straight sets 6-2, 6-1. “Our sole victory was a beautifully played match at #1 doubles by the new team of Gianluca Bini and Luca LaForte. They trounced their opponents, they played exceptionally well. We have a lot of confidence in this duo for the remainder of the season,” Landes said. 6-1 to O’Dowd In singles, Smolko won 7-5, 7-5 at No. 1. Nate Welch lost 6-3, 6-3 at No. 2, Nick King fell 6-3, 6-4 at No. 3, while freshman Emilio Misra lost in three sets at No. 4, 3-6, 6-1, 7-5. Misra had a chance to win the match at No. 4, but fell narrowly short. “Emilio split sets and then had two match points in the third, eventually losing it 7 -5. He played very well at times but just needed a little more offensive play to close it out,” Landes said. In doubles, Will Tenney and LaForte lost at No. 1, 6-2, 6-1. Kasper Jansson and Bini fell 6-3, 6-2 at No. 2, while Ben Davis and Hunter Fasteau lost in three sets at No. 3, 4-6, 6-0, 7-6 (7-4). 6-1 to Lick-Wilmerding Smolko lost at No. 1 in a heated three-set match with the 10-point super breaker third set going an extra few points, 4-6, 7-5, 13-11. “There were three matches that could have gone our way. articles.text: The Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Archive’s (BAMPFA) West Coast engagement of Making Their Mark: Works from the Shah Garg Collection, an exhibition of one of the largest private collections of work by women artists, is on view now through April 20. Making Their Mark brings together more than seventy artworks from the Shah Garg Collection and features artists from the postwar period to the present day, as well as artists with deep ties to the Bay Area, including Mary Corse, Trude Guermonprez, Mary Heilmann, Mary Lovelace O’Neal, Elizabeth Murray, and Kay Sekimachi. Also featured are internationally distinguished artists including Lynda Benglis, Barbara Chase-Riboud, Sonya Gomes, Maria Lassnig, Joan Mitchell, Julie Mehretu, Howardena Pindell, Jaune Quick-to-See Smith, and more. BAMPFA’s display is the first public presentation of this exhibition following its premiere in New York in 2023 and was assembled by the Bay Area philanthropist Komal Shah and her husband Gaurav Garg. “The significant investment in the work of women artists by Komal and Gaurav is truly inspiring and groundbreaking,” said BAMPFA’s Executive Director Julie Rodrigues Widholm. “We are so grateful that their vision dovetails with ours at BAMPFA to create public access to such excellent examples of artwork by leading artists of our time, which will generate new scholarship and new art histories for years to come.” “The Shah Garg Foundation is honored to bring Making Their Mark to an institution as brilliant as Berkeley and further educate a younger generation on the accomplishments of women artists,” said Shah. “We are filled with so much excitement at the opportunity to spotlight works that have rarely been seen before to this community. To learn more, and to purchase tickets, visit https://bampfa.org/ making-their-mark. articles.text: Grand Parade is Sunday, April 20 The 58th annual Northern California Cherry Blossom Festival (NCCBF) is coming back to San Francisco’s Japantown on Saturday, April 12, with a host of activities open to the public that weekend and the following weekend. NCCBF is California’s most prominent celebration of Japanese and Japanese American culture as well as the largest Cherry Blossom Festival on the West Coast. The free festival draws over 220,000 visitors annually over two weekends in April to celebrate the arrival of spring and tout the city’s stunning sakura displays. The first Northern California Cherry Blossom Festival, formerly called the San Francisco Cherry Blossom Festival, was celebrated over three days in March 1968 after the opening of the Japan Trade Center, now Japan Center Malls, in the city’s Japantown on March 28, 1968. The festival is now organized by a group of volunteers and has grown to become one of the largest and most prominent cherry blossom festivals outside of Japan. The event features live music and cultural performances, pop-up arts and crafts by local vendors and artists, Japanese cuisine food trucks and a Sapporo beer garden. Guests can learn more information about the festival from community and sponsor information booths and participate in interactive, family-friendly activities at the Children’s Cherry Blossom Village on Post Street outside the Kinokuniya Mall. The final San Francisco screening of KINTSUKUROI, a film that follows members of the Ito family from their pre-war life in Japantown to the concentration 2019 Northern California Cherry Blossom Festival Grand Parade in San Francisco’s Japantown camps of the American West, is held on Sunday, April 13, at the Kabuki Cinema as part of the NCCBF. The festival concludes with a grand parade, the highlight of the NCCBF, which stretches over a mile from Civic Center Plaza to Japantown. The parade showcases cultural and community organizations that contribute to the continued success of the festival, and features a procession of traditional taiko drummers, dancers and decorative floats. The parade is held on Sunday, April 20, departing from San Francisco’s Civic Center Plaza at 1:00 p.m., proceeding up Polk Street to Post Street, and ending in Japantown at Post and Fillmore Streets. While Japantown is the epicenter of the upcoming festival, be sure to visit the Japanese Tea Garden in Golden Gate Park to view magnificent cherry blossom displays. Sakura blossoms are blooming in the garden and can be seen by the Main Gate, Tea House, and Drum Bridge until early April. All events are free and open to the public. Visit https://sfcherryblossom.org/schedule/ to learn more and for a full list of programming. articles.text: Photo courtesy Dallas Museum of Art Kunié Sugiura, Sidewalk Palms, 1980 An exhibition featuring over 60 works by Japanese American photoartist Kunie Sugiura opens at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) on April 26. Japanese native Sugiura pioneered a unique category of artistic expression by blending photography with painting, drawing and other mediums. She also experimented with the photogram technique, one of the earliest forms of photography dating back to 1839. Kunié Sugiura: Photopainting, her first survey exhibition in the U.S., features over 60 artworks spanning her sixty-decades long career. “Throughout her career, Kunié Sugiura has subverted traditional notions of photography, bravely bucking trends to produce a distinctive body of work that is unmistakably her own,” said Erin O’Toole, SFMOMA’s curator and head of photography. “Sugiura’s many experiments and explorations with the photographic medium upend our notions of what photography can be,” added SFMOMA Director Christopher Bedford. “We look forward to engaging our communities with KuniéSugiura’s art and are honored to open the first survey exhibition of her work in the U.S.” Sugiura moved to the U.S. in 1963 to study at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago where she was a mentee of conceptual artist and photographer Kenneth Josephson. A major retrospective of her art was on display at the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum in 2018. From 1986 to 2008 she produced a column entitled “New York Report,” in which she reviewed gallery and museum exhibitions, for the Japanese-language magazine Bijutsu Techo. “I am very happy I found a way of life that has interested me and has kept my focus for so long,” Sugiura said in an interview with Cristina Chan, SFMOMA’s Managing Editor. “Over my career, I have had a few people and audiences who have supported my art. This time, I feel like more people are understanding my ideas and art.” Kunié Sugiura: Photopainting is on display from April 26 to September 14. Guests at SFMOMA’s Art Bash on April 23 will enjoy a sneak peek of the exhibition. Visit https://www.sfmoma.org/ exhibition/kunie-sugiura-photopainting/ to learn more. ®

articles.text: San Francisco Symphony musicians perform the score of 1997 mega blockbuster Titanic this Friday and Saturday. San Francisco Symphony musicians will perform the Titanic score live alongside a screening of the film at Davies Symphony Hall this Friday, April 4 and Saturday, April 5. The 1997 mega blockbuster Titanic features an iconic score composed, orchestrated, and conducted by James Horner. The film’s immense success allowed the soundtrack to shoot to the top of the charts and sell over 27 million copies worldwide, making it one of the top 100 best-selling albums in the United States. Celine Dion’s “My Heart Will Go On”, the film’s signature song written by James Horner and Will Jennings, won the 1997 Academy Award for Best Original Song as well as the Golden Globe Award for Best Original Song in 1998. Performances are conducted by Sarah Hicks and feature vocalist Alice Zawadzki and the San Francisco Girls Chorus accompanying the orchestra. Guests will enjoy a blue Heart of the Ocean cocktail and Sweet Heart of the Ocean macarons inspired by the film, offered at the Davies Symphony Hall bar. The Friday performance begins at 7:30 p.m.; the Saturday, April 5 performance begins at 2 p.m. Visit https://www.sfsymphony. org/Buy-Tickets/2024-25/Titanic to purchase tickets, or call the box office at 415-864-6000.

articles.text: Shotgun Players current production of Yasmina Reza’s Art is now extended through Saturday, April 12, with an added matinee performance and closing final performance at 8:00 p.m. Reza’s internationally-acclaimed play launched Shotgun Players 33rd season with direction by Emilie Whelan. Art, written in French and adapted to English, premiered at Comédie des Champs-Élysées in Paris in 1994 and won a Tony Award for best play in 1998 and the Olivier Award for best comedy in 1997. The English-language adaptation, translated by Christopher Hampton and directed by Matthew Warchus, opened in London’s West End in 1996. Art explores dy namics between lifelong friends Serge, Marc, and Yvan as their relationships slowly unravel when Serge, played by Benoît Monin, purchases a $200,000 piece of modern art. Marc, played by David Sinaiko, questions his friend’s extravagant purchase, likening it to a mid-life crisis, while neutral Yvan attempts to mediate arguments between them. Eventually, the painting begins to symbolize Serge, Marc, and Yvan’s own perceived failures. “That painting is the first crack for the wall to come tumbling down,” Whelan said. “[Reza] bears these cracks in the wall [and] lines in the canvas through a mad hilarity. She stretches her comedy, kneads it and rolls it out to a place of absurdity, and in 2025 that feels about right.” “The play makes me think about the trade-offs we make in the intimate relationships we engage in,” Shotgun’s Artistic Director Patrick Dooley added. “Platonic [or] romantic, and how we are sometimes asked to compromise our integrity and our values in order to maintain those relationships. Would you be willing to compromise your integrity, your values, in the name of ‘art’?” Art is showing onstage at the Ashby Stage in Berkeley now through April 12, Wednesdays and Thursdays at 7:00 p.m., Fridays and Saturdays at 8:00 p.m. and Sundays at 2:00 p.m. Visit www.shotgunplayers.org or call the box office at (510) 841- 6500 ext. 303 to purchase tickets. pages.text: Wednesday, April 2, 2025 17 Kunié Sugiura exhibition opens at SFMOMA April 26 Photo courtesy Dallas Museum of Art Kunié Sugiura, Sidewalk Palms, 1980 By Allyson Aleksey An exhibition featuring over 60 works by Japanese American photoartist Kunie Sugiura opens at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) on April 26. Japanese native Sugiura pioneered a unique category of artistic expression by blending photography with painting, drawing and other mediums. She also experimented with the photogram technique, one of the earliest forms of photography dating back to 1839. Kunié Sugiura: Photopainting, her first survey exhibition in the U.S., features over 60 artworks spanning her sixty-decades long career. “Throughout her career, Kunié Sugiura has subverted traditional notions of photography, bravely bucking trends to produce a distinctive body of work that is unmistakably her own,” said Erin O’Toole, SFMOMA’s curator and head of photography. “Sugiura’s many experiments and explorations with the photographic medium upend our notions of what photography can be,” added SFMOMA Director Christopher Bedford. “We look forward to engaging our communities with KuniéSugiura’s art and are honored to open the first survey exhibition of her work in the U.S.” Sugiura moved to the U.S. in 1963 to study at the School of the Art Institute of Chicago where she was a mentee of conceptual artist and photographer Kenneth Josephson. A major retrospective of her art was on display at the Tokyo Photographic Art Museum in 2018. From 1986 to 2008 she produced a column entitled “New York Report,” in which she reviewed gallery and museum exhibitions, for the Japanese-language magazine Bijutsu Techo. “I am very happy I found a way of life that has interested me and has kept my focus for so long,” Sugiura said in an interview with Cristina Chan, SFMOMA’s Managing Editor. “Over my career, I have had a few people and audiences who have supported my art. This time, I feel like more people are understanding my ideas and art.” Kunié Sugiura: Photopainting is on display from April 26 to September 14. Guests at SFMOMA’s Art Bash on April 23 will enjoy a sneak peek of the exhibition. articles.text: Sona Jobarteh Gambian multi-instrumentalist, singer and composer Sona Jobarteh performs at the Herbst Theatre in San Francisco this Friday, April 4. Called “a griot for a new generation of West Africans” by BBC Radio, Jobarteh is regarded as a master and a pioneer of the kora, a unique 21-string African lute. Most similar to a lute or a harp, the kora is played almost exclusively in West Africa and was first discovered in the Gambia. Music for the kora was not written until the 20th century. Songs are passed down from griots, composed of West African storytellers, singers, musicians, and oral historians. Griots also keep records of all births, deaths, marriages through the generations of the village and pass traditionally composed music down to younger generations. Gambian griot traditions date back nearly seven centuries. Jobarteh, born in London, is from one of only five principal kora-playing ‘griot’ families of West Africa and is the first female professional kora player to come from a griot family. She is the granddaughter of the griot of her line, Amadu Bansang Jobarteh, whose father migrated from Mali to Gambia. Jobarteh’s cousin is celebrated kora player Toumani Diabaté and her brother Tunde Jegede is also a renowned diaspora kora player. Jobar teh’s debut album Afro-Acoustic Soul, released in 2008, is influenced heavily by her Gambian background but also includes melodies that could be heard on more conventional European radio stations. Her second album and first solo recording Fasiya, released in 2011, highlighted her skills as a vocalist and multi-instrumentalist. She returns to SF JAZZ next month following the release of her 2022 follow-up for African Guild Records, Badinyaa Kumoo. Jobarteh performs at the Herbst Theatre, an auditorium in the War Memorial and Performing Arts Center in San Francisco’s Civic Center, on Friday, April 4. The concert begins at 8 p.m. Visit https://www.sfjazz.org/ tickets/productions/24-25/sona-jobarteh/ to purchase tickets.

articles.text: Tom Cruise, indisputably a top-tier movie star since his iconic Risky Business slide, continues his resilient career with a variety of films, though he’s best known for the Mission: Impossible franchise and Top Gun. This brings us to Knight and Day, a romantic comedy where Cruise portrays rogue government agent Roy Miller, alongside Cameron Diaz as June Havens, an unsuspecting traveler en route from Wichita to Boston. June’s suitcase, oddly, contains retro muscle car parts. A seemingly chance encounter at the Wichita airport thrusts June into a whirlwind of danger, as both good and bad people seek to kill Roy. June attempts to maintain composure, often succumbing to unconsciousness—a recurring gag that is surprisingly charming. The film, surprisingly, is entertaining. What could have been a cynical attempt to package two attractive movie stars in a silly nonstarter is a breezy, enjoyable ride. Knight and Day also features a compelling MacGuffin, an object that quickly captures attention. The film cleverly plays with audience expectations, revealing unexpected layers to both Roy and June. Their dynamic evolves beyond simple romantic comedy tropes, adding a layer of intrigue. The twists and turns keep the audience guessing, and the film’s playful tone ensures that even the most outlandish scenarios remain engaging. While the plot may seem straightforward, a closer look reveals subtle clues and motivations that add depth to the characters’ actions. The film’s strength lies in its ability to balance action, comedy, and romance without sacrificing its sense of fun. Knight and Day. Directed by James Mangold. 20th Century Studios/ Bontonfilm A.S. . June attempts to maintain composure, often succumbing to unconsciousness—a recurring gag that is surprisingly charming. The film, surprisingly, is entertaining. What could have been a cynical attempt to package two attractive movie stars in a silly nonstarter is a breezy, enjoyable ride. Knight and Day also features a compelling MacGuffin, an object that quickly captures attention. The film cleverly plays with audience expectations, revealing unexpected layers to both Roy and June. Their dynamic evolves beyond simple romantic comedy tropes, adding a layer of intrigue. While the plot may seem straightforward, a closer look reveals subtle clues and motivations that add depth to the characters’ actions. articles.text: The Quiet Girl has been referred to as a whisper of a film, and it is that and so much more. Based on a 2010 novella by Claire Keegan and nominated for an Oscar in the Best International Feature Film category, the Irish film is an unassuming, beautifully acted and photographed coming-of-age drama about a nine-year-old girl named Cait (Catherine Clinch). The film opens with Cait lying in a lush field, hidden, looking up at a blue sky. A voice in the distance is calling her name. We soon discover that she lives with an impoverished farm family where, to her shame she occasionally wets her bed and is harshly ignored by both her parents (Kate Nic Chonaonaigh and Michael Patric) and her siblings. School is also a struggle, something to be endured, a place where she is often ridiculed by her schoolmates. Cait’s father, Da, is shiftless, preferring to spend time in a local pub drinking his pint than preparing for the seasonal harvest. Finding it difficult to feed all the children (Cait’s mother, Mam, is again pregnant), the parents decide to send Cait to spend the summer with a distant cousin, Eibhlin (Carey Crowley), and her husband Sean (Andrew Bennett), who are rural dairy farmers. Da drives her to the distant farm, saying little, and is so disengaged that when he leaves Cait with the Catherine Clinch and Carrie Crowley in The Quiet Girl couple, absent even a goodbye, he drives off with her suitcase still in the trunk of the car. It’s with this couple (it takes Sean a bit longer than Eibhlin to warm up to the girl) she experiences a kindness and generosity, attention and concern that she has never felt before. Cait comes to realize, slowly, tentatively, that there is a world which is far different from the one she has known. Expecting indifference or cruelty, she discovers the opposite. Her reflexive response to life, is slowly abandoned and Cait begins to blossom. The Quiet Girl is a beautiful film, gentle and moving, subtle yet deeply emotive. It is a narrative about the power of kindness that is all too often underrated. When encountered, it can heal, even delight, and be transformative. As it does with Cait. The Quiet Girl. articles.text: Spirited Away, directed by Hayao Miyazaki, is an award-winning animated film that captivates audiences with its compelling fairytale-adventure. The film won an Oscar, a Golden Bear and an Annie Award. The narrative centers on 10-year-old Chihiro (Daveigh Chase), who is unhappy about her family’s move to the countryside. Her mother (Lauren Holly) and father (Michael Chiklis) take a wrong turn and discover what appears to be an abandoned amusement park. When her parents begin eating at a restaurant, Chihiro wanders off and meets Haku (Jason Marsden), a boy who shows her around. Upon returning, she finds her parents transformed into pigs. Haku explains that a witch named Yubaba (Suzanne Pleshette), who runs a bathhouse for spirits, is responsible. He warns Chihiro to avoid Yubaba, but Chihiro learns she must work for the witch to save her parents. Chihiro’s journey through the spirit world introduces her to dragons, frog-men, a giant baby, a spidery furnace stoker and other creatures. The film focuses on Chihiro’s transformation as she learns to be brave for herself and her parents. The animation is visually rich, with each frame resembling a hand-drawn work of art. The story, rooted in Japanese mythology, may appeal more to young girls, but boys will also enjoy the mysterious spirits, particularly Yubaba. Spirited Away. Written and directed by Hayao Miyazaki. articles.text: The Piedmont Flix Fest’s selection, Amelie, directed by Jean-Pierre Jeunet, embodies a bellowed French charm. Amelie stars Audrey Tautou, who may remind some viewers of Audrey Hepburn. pages.text: 22 Wednesday, April 2, 2025 Walking on Wednesday Wed. Walkers honor women’s history, local legacy By Dick Carter Last Wednesday marked the final Wednesday of March, the first Wednesday of spring, and the last chance this year for the Walking on Wednesdays group to celebrate Women’s History Month. With clear skies and a spring breeze, the occasion drew 50 walkers and six K-9 companions for their weekly gathering. Women’s History Month began in 1981 when Congress authorized the President to proclaim the week beginning March 7, 1982, as Women’s History Week. Over the next several years, Congress passed annual resolutions recognizing the week. In 1987, after advocacy from the Last week’s gathering of the Walking on Wednesdays group included Albert Chen, Jim Kuo, Denny McGee, Tracy Lee, Kathlene Henrickson with K-9 best friends Finn and Frankie, Quincy Dong, Debbie Powell, Sylvia Fones, Mike Henn with K-9 best friend Roger, Rick Eigenbrode, Edith Lee, Ken Moy, June Yee, Phil Witte, Laura DuDell-Foley, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Lori Austin, Bob Wong, Karin Fetherston with K-9 best friend Gwen, Alissa Quan, Helen Dong, Susan Anderson, Carolyn George, Dave DeRoche, Joyce Hicks with K-9 best friend Mocha, Liza Dalrymple, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper, Mark Davis, Sarah Johnson, Jim Kellogg, Leigh Sorensen with K-9 best friend McDuff, Nancy Henn, Chuck Oraftik, Lois Price, Irene Thompson, Claudine Bach, Abha Kothari, Bill Ahern, Melba Yee, Lisa Euphrat, Michelle Yang, Noemi Alvarado, Vicki Trimbach, Brenda Ferrero, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to welcome Gerry Montmorency, John Kelson, and Dick Anderson who were walking with them for the first time. National Women’s History Project, March was officially designated Women’s History Month – and has been celebrated as such ever since. In Piedmont, women’s contributions to the community abound. One such story, shared during the walk, was drawn from an article by Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombardi in the Piedmont Post. The group revisited the tale of the Miss Ransom and Miss Bridges School for Girls, the city’s first school. Fittingly, Lombardi was honored this March with the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Betty C. Howard Award, which recognizes dedication to the community. The award is named for Betty C. Howard, the longtime Recreation Department secretary during the mid-20th century. The walk began with a pause to admire blooming tulips around the Exedra vase, then wound through upper Piedmont Park and past Community Hall, where more tulips greeted the group. From there, walkers made their way to the corner of Highland Avenue and Hazel Lane, near the original site of Amy Requa Long’s pioneering school. In the early 1900s Long sought a quality education for her daughters and convinced her father, Isaac Requa – who made his fortune in banking, mining, and railroads – to build a one-room schoolhouse on his estate, “The Highlands.” The school eventually outgrew its modest beginnings, prompting Long to lease a home at Highland and Hazel Lane and hire teachers Marion Ransom and Edith Bridges from Berkeley’s Anna Head School. As enrollment grew, Long commissioned famed architect Julia Morgan in 1908 to design a new school building on five acres of what is now Hazel Lane. The Miss Ransom and Miss Bridges School for Girls officially opened in 1913, complete with classrooms, dormitories, and eventually a gymnasium. At its height, the school served students from first grade through high school and attracted girls from prominent California families. But like many institutions, the school was hit hard by the Great Depression. Enrollment fell, and the school closed in 1932. Its buildings were demolished in 1936, and the property was later developed by architect Albert Farr into what is now Ransom Gardens. The Wednesday group followed Hazel Lane to the redwood tree at 71 Hazel Lane—the former entrance to the school—then continued to 141 Hazel Lane, where a Farr-designed home now stands. They posed for a group photo in front of the house and admired the area’s history, including Piedmont’s first Hazel Lane home, built in 1937 at No. 152. articles.text: Former longtime Piedmont resident Suzanne Vinson Royce passed away peacefully on March 8, 2025 near her home in Healdsburg, California after a brief illness. She was 89. Suzy was born in Oakland California on December 26, 1935, to Virginia Pearson Vinson and Eugene Mulally Vinson. She is predeceased by her husband, Richard Ernest Royce and her older sister, Nancy Vinson Rubey of Diablo. She attended Bentley School in Berkeley, Our Lady of Lourdes in Oakland, Oakland High School, and graduated from San Ramon Valley High School in Danville. Suzy attended the University of California at Berkeley where she was a member of the Chi Omega Sorority. Suzy started a small and successful manufacturing business on Piedmont Avenue. She returned to Cal to complete her studies and received a degree in Fine Arts. She worked for a time at the Philips Collection in Washington, D. C. and then returned to the Bay Area where she continued to manage her Piedmont Avenue business and work as an independent Art Consultant. Proceeds from the tastings will go toward projects and events like the Safety Ambassador Program and the Montclair Beer, Wine and Music Festival. Taste of Montclair Village is also supported by the Montclair Cares Club, which provides additional funds and support for the MVA’s mission and operations. One of the main urban design and architectural objections to different uses, types and sizes of buildings next to each other is the abruptness of change. This is especially true in residential areas, where people live. For example, think of a new seven-story glass clad office building located in a two story residential neighborhood – clearly not appropriate. Wednesday Walkers Continued from page 22 Next, the walkers headed up Requa Place, a cul-de-sac leading to the former site of The Highlands mansion, before looping back down Highland Avenue and ascending Caperton Way. They took a scenic turn onto Sheridan and Lakeview Avenues, eventually arriving at Poplar Way—a hidden lane with a street sign but no addresses or poplar trees, just a charming path behind Mountain and Lakeview homes. The walk wrapped up with a gentle descent down Mountain Avenue and along a 217-foot path to Sierra Avenue, before returning to the Exedra. It was, as always, a walk filled with camaraderie, curiosity, and community pride—this time with a special nod to the many women who have shaped Piedmont’s past. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge.
